# Osteoarthritis of the hip and knee

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > Lower extremity > Osteoarthritis of the hip and knee*

[Original Article Link](/library/LQ0w9f)

---

## Summary

<u>Osteoarthritis</u> of the hip and knee is characterized by <u>joint</u> degeneration, which can lead to functional impairment. Although the exact etiology is unknown, <u>risk factors</u> include older age, overuse of the <u>joint</u>, <u>obesity</u>, previous injuries, and asymmetrically stressed <u>joints</u>. Patients often present with <u>joint</u> stiffness and <u>pain</u>, which can progress to severe <u>pain</u> and functional limitation. <u>Osteoarthritis</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>, supported by radiological findings. Initial management includes nonpharmacological measures such as weight loss, <u>physical therapy</u>, and the use of assistive devices (e.g., canes, <u>braces</u>), and short-term pharmacotherapy for <u>pain management</u>. If <u>conservative measures</u> do not improve the patient's quality of life and <u>joint</u> destruction is severe, surgical procedures such as <u>arthroplasty</u> may be indicated.




For more general information on <u>osteoarthritis</u>, see the respective article.

---

## Epidemiology

The risk of developing hip and knee <u>osteoarthritis</u> increases with age.  [[1]](/library/0Jaesl)[[2]](/library/aJaQsl)




* Age: Peak <u>incidence</u> at initial diagnosis is 50–60 years of age.

* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u>, especially in patients older than 50 years





> [!TIP]
> <u>Osteoarthritis</u> is the most common disease of the <u>hip joint</u> in adults.




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* See “Etiology” in <u>osteoarthritis</u>. [[3]](/library/S-ay9M)

* <u>Primary osteoarthritis</u>: <u>idiopathic</u>

* <u>Secondary osteoarthritis</u>

* Hip <u>osteoarthritis</u> due to <u>Legg-Calvé-Perthes</u> disease, <u>slipped capital femoral epiphysis</u>, <u>developmental dysplasia of the hip</u>, <u>hemochromatosis</u>, <u>gout</u>, stiffened <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>knee joint</u>

* Knee <u>osteoarthritis</u> due to <u>genu valgum</u>, <u>genu varum</u>, cruciate <u>ligament</u> rupture, <u>meniscal tear</u>

---

## Clinical features

See also "<u>Clinical features of osteoarthritis</u>.” [[4]](/library/h-acCM)




* Hip <u>osteoarthritis</u>

* <u>Pain</u> in the groin area and above the greater trochanter

* Increased <u>contracture</u> in the flexor, <u>external rotation</u>, and <u>adduction</u> position → <u>antalgic gait</u>

* Early signs: limited and painful <u>internal rotation</u> of the hip <u>joint</u>

* <u>Pain</u> on palpation: greater trochanter, groin

* Positive Thomas test

* Function: test for hip <u>flexion</u> <u>contracture</u>

* Position: <u>supine</u>

* Procedure: Examiner passively flexes the <u>hip joint</u> opposite to the affected side to a maximum to compensate lumbar <u>lordosis</u>.

* Positive test: If <u>flexion</u> <u>contracture</u> is present, the <u>ipsilateral</u> leg will simultaneously flex independently as a reflex.

* Knee <u>osteoarthritis</u>

* Function-limiting <u>knee pain</u>

* Knee swelling which increases on activity

* Mechanical instability, locking, catching sensation

* In case of patello-femoral <u>osteoarthritis</u>: positive Patellar grind test (<u>pain</u> on movement of the patella)

* <u>Cartilage</u> damage usually begins medially and may lead to <u>genu varum</u> (bowing of legs)





> [!TIP]
> Walking downhill is painful with knee <u>osteoarthritis</u>, whereas walking uphill is painful with hip <u>osteoarthritis</u>!

---

## Diagnosis

<u>Osteoarthritis</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>. Diagnostic studies may be indicated if there is clinical uncertainty or to exclude alternative diagnoses (see “<u>Diagnosis of osteoarthritis</u>” and “<u>Differential diagnoses of inflammatory arthritis</u>”). [[5]](/library/Gj1BbS0)




### <u>Plain radiography</u> [[5]](/library/Gj1BbS0)




* Patient position: Obtain multiple views (e.g., anteroposterior, <u>lateral</u>) of the affected <u>joints</u>, if possible. [[6]](/library/n417PS0)

* Hip: Patient may be <u>weight-bearing</u> or <u>non-weight-bearing</u>.

* Knee: Patient should be standing.

* Supportive findings

* <u>Radiological signs of osteoarthritis</u>  [[5]](/library/Gj1BbS0)

* Standing views of the knee may show: [[6]](/library/n417PS0)

* <u>Joint</u> space narrowing

* Uneven pressure distribution: e.g., patella lateralization, <u>genu valgum</u>, <u>genu varum</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>X-rays</u> may appear normal in the early stages of <u>osteoarthritis</u>. The absence of <u>radiological signs of osteoarthritis</u> does not rule out <u>osteoarthritis</u>. [[5]](/library/Gj1BbS0)

### Additional studies [[5]](/library/Gj1BbS0)




Consider to rule out complications and alternative diagnoses (e.g., <u>fractures</u>, infection), and for surgical planning. [[5]](/library/Gj1BbS0)[[6]](/library/n417PS0)




* Imaging

* <u>MRI</u>, <u>ultrasound</u>, or <u>CT scan</u> of the affected <u>joint</u>

* See “Other imaging modalities” and “Further investigations” in “<u>Diagnostics of osteoarthritis</u>.”

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: usually normal in <u>osteoarthritis</u>  [[7]](/library/kl1mCS0)

---

## Treatment

### Approach [[8]](/library/_yX5300)[[9]](/library/hMdcoq0)




* Recommend nonpharmacological management for all patients (see “<u>Management of osteoarthritis</u>”).

* Initiate pharmacological therapy for <u>pain management</u>, as needed.

* Indications for referral to orthopedic <u>surgery</u> include:

* Persistent symptoms despite multiple trials of <u>conservative management</u> [[5]](/library/Gj1BbS0)

* Symptoms associated with radiographic evidence of <u>osteonecrosis</u> or moderate-to-severe <u>osteoarthritis</u>   [[9]](/library/hMdcoq0)





### <u>Conservative management</u> [[5]](/library/Gj1BbS0)[[10]](/library/DQ11yg0)




* Nonpharmacological management [[8]](/library/_yX5300)[[10]](/library/DQ11yg0)

* Weight loss (if <u>overweight or obese</u>) and exercise  are recommended for all patients.

* <u>Physical therapy</u> and use of assistive devices (e.g., cane, knee <u>braces</u>) may help improve <u>pain</u> and mobility.

* There is limited evidence to support the routine use of oral supplements (e.g., fish oil, <u>vitamin D</u>, glucosamine, <u>chondroitin sulfate</u>)  or <u>orthotic insoles</u>.  [[5]](/library/Gj1BbS0)[[8]](/library/_yX5300)[[10]](/library/DQ11yg0)[[11]](/library/wQ1hyg0)

* Pharmacotherapy [[5]](/library/Gj1BbS0)

* First line: <u>NSAIDs</u>

* Patients who cannot tolerate or do not improve with <u>NSAIDs</u>: See “<u>Management of osteoarthritis</u>” for alternative agents.

* <u>Intraarticular glucocorticoid injection</u>: Consider for local, short-term relief in patients with <u>osteoarthritis</u> of the hip and knee.

* Intraarticular <u>triamcinolone</u> DOSAGE or <u>methylprednisolone</u> DOSAGE [[12]](/library/vZcAWa0)

* Use <u>ultrasound</u> to guide <u>hip joint</u> injections.

* Risks: <u>cartilage</u> loss, <u>joint</u> space infection

* Intraarticular <u>hyaluronic acid</u>: may be considered for <u>osteoarthritis</u> of the knee  [[8]](/library/_yX5300)[[11]](/library/wQ1hyg0)[[13]](/library/_Q15Ag0)





> [!TIP]
> Pharmacotherapy should only be used as a short-term treatment in symptomatic patients; long-term therapy is associated with many adverse effects.




### <u>Surgery</u>




#### <u>Arthroplasty</u>




* Total or partial <u>joint</u> replacement may be considered for advanced <u>joint</u> destruction with <u>pain</u> and functional impairment not adequately controlled by <u>conservative management</u>. [[5]](/library/Gj1BbS0)

* Type of <u>surgery</u> depends on the <u>joint</u> involved and the extent of involvement; indications include:

* <u>Total hip arthroplasty</u>

* Primary and <u>secondary osteoarthritis</u> of the hip

* <u>Femoral neck fracture</u> in patients with concomitant <u>osteoarthritis</u> [[14]](/library/M41MPS0)[[15]](/library/0M1eMh0)

* <u>Total knee replacement</u>: <u>osteoarthritis</u> of one or more compartments of <u>the knee joint</u> [[16]](/library/BQ1zyg0)[[17]](/library/VM1Gnh0)

* <u>Partial knee replacement</u>: isolated <u>osteoarthritis</u> of one or two compartments of <u>the knee joint</u> [[6]](/library/n417PS0)[[16]](/library/BQ1zyg0)[[17]](/library/VM1Gnh0)

* See also “<u>Complications after arthroplasty</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> Patients undergoing <u>total joint replacement</u> should receive <u>perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis</u> and <u>VTE prophylaxis</u>. Early postoperative <u>physiotherapy</u> can reduce the duration of hospitalization and improve <u>pain</u> and function. See “Perioperative considerations” in “<u>Treatment of osteoarthritis</u>” for details. [[18]](/library/bebHxs)




#### <u>Osteotomy</u>




* May be considered to delay the development or worsening of <u>osteoarthritis</u> in young individuals (< 60 years of age) with unicompartmental <u>osteoarthritis</u> (e.g., due to trauma)  [[10]](/library/DQ11yg0)[[16]](/library/BQ1zyg0)[[19]](/library/-yXD300)

* Types and indications include:

* High tibial <u>osteotomy</u>: <u>osteoarthritis</u> of the <u>medial</u> compartment of the knee and associated genu varus

* Low <u>femoral osteotomy</u>: <u>osteoarthritis</u> of the <u>lateral</u> compartment of the knee and associated <u>genu valgum</u>

* <u>Hip osteotomy</u>: <u>hip dysplasia</u> and no significant <u>osteoarthritis</u>





#### <u>Arthroscopy</u>



* Consider for <u>osteoarthritis</u> and a concomitant <u>meniscal tear</u> that does not respond to <u>conservative management</u> [[10]](/library/DQ11yg0)[[19]](/library/-yXD300)
